## Status: reviewed and implemented; DFTK comparison pending
Reviewed on 2026-11-11. The review is kept at `reviews/review_02b_scf_silicon.md`.
It rebuilt the method independently from this post (a NumPy plane-wave LDA)
and reproduced every number quoted here. It found one physics error: the
FFT-grid condition for the symmetry of diamond is $N$ even, not $4 \mid N$.
It also changed the argument for the Γ-centred grid, the evidence for buffer
bands and the form of the projector protocol, and answered the open
questions. The decisions are recorded at the [end of this
post](#decisions-from-review).

The [validation document](../validation/02b_scf_silicon.qmd) confirms the
post's numbers and corrects three expectations that were measured with the
2a per-k-point gap guard. With the guard over the whole grid:

- the displaced force-test geometry is nearly gapless on the 2³ grid
  (0.12 mHa), so its tests run on the 3³ grid;
- silicon without XC is a semimetal on these grids, so the XC-off net-force
  control runs without the guard;
- local-only silicon is rejected, as stated below, but its SCF does not
  converge either, so "a converged state" overstates what the 2a SCF found.

It also refines two statements. Only the upper valence bands agree closely
with Cohen–Bergstresser; the lowest does not. And 6³ is within about 0.2 mHa
of the k-converged energy, not 0.5. The DFTK comparison follows
implementation, as in 2a.

Formulas marked *checked* were verified numerically while the post was being
prepared, and again by the review. Numbers quoted "from the throwaway check"
come from a scratch nonlocal term run through the 2a SCF; numbers quoted
"from the review" come from the review's independent code.
:::

## Scope

Milestone 2b takes the 2a machinery from a molecule at Γ to a bulk
semiconductor. The test system is diamond-structure silicon with the HGH LDA
pseudopotential [@hgh1998], spin-unpolarised, with Slater + PW92 as in 2a.
Two things are new physics, and both are needed at once, because silicon has
neither a local-only pseudopotential nor a usable energy at Γ alone (the
Γ-only energy is 0.63 Ha off, and the Γ-only gap is 2.13 eV against 0.47 eV):

- **Nonlocal projectors.** The HGH silicon pseudopotential has separable
  projectors in the $s$ and $p$ channels. They enter the Hamiltonian as a new
  operator term, the energy as its expectation value, and the pseudopotential
  protocol as new reciprocal-space radial data.
- **Brillouin-zone sampling.** A uniform k-grid with weights, the density and
  energy as weighted sums over it, and occupations, the gap guard and the
  weight derivatives defined over all k-points rather than per k-point.

On top of these:

- the SCF total energy of silicon, its convergence with cutoff and k-grid,
  and the energy–volume curve,
- forces from `jax.grad` with the nonlocal term, at a displaced geometry,
- Kohn–Sham bands along a path from the converged density, compared with the
  Cohen–Bergstresser bands of [1b](01b_cohen_bergstresser.qmd),
- the design of the DFTK comparison, run after implementation as in 2a.

Out of scope: metals and smearing, reduction of the k-grid by symmetry,
spin polarisation and spin–orbit coupling, nonlinear core corrections, GGA,
stress as a physical quantity (the Pulay stress is discussed but not
corrected), phonons and other second derivatives, implicit differentiation
through the SCF, and quasiparticle corrections to the band gap.

Everything not mentioned is as in the [2a post](02a_scf_h2.qmd): the FFT
grid and its rule, Hartree, XC, Ewald, the $\mathbf{G}=0$ conventions, the
direct energy functional, `solve(F, ρ₀)` with Anderson mixing, and LOBPCG.
Atomic units throughout; band energies are converted to eV, and lattice
constants to Å, only at the output boundary.

## The separable nonlocal pseudopotential

A norm-conserving pseudopotential acts differently on each angular momentum
(see the [concept post](../concepts/pseudopotentials.qmd)). The GTH/HGH form
[@gth1996; @hgh1998] writes the $l$-dependent part as a sum of separable
projectors, in the manner of Kleinman and Bylander [@kleinman_bylander1982],
on top of the local part of 2a. For one atom at the origin,

$$
V_\text{nl}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') = \sum_{l}\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\sum_{i,j}
Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{r}})\,p_i^l(r)\;h_{ij}^l\;p_j^l(r')\,Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}'),
$$

with real spherical harmonics $Y_{lm}$, a real symmetric coupling matrix
$h^l$ per channel, and Gaussian radial projectors

$$
p_i^l(r) = \frac{\sqrt2\; r^{\,l+2(i-1)}\, e^{-r^2/2r_l^2}}
{r_l^{\,l+(4i-1)/2}\,\sqrt{\Gamma\!\big(l+\tfrac{4i-1}{2}\big)}},
\qquad \int_0^\infty p_i^l(r)^2\,r^2\,dr = 1 .
$$

The normalisation was *checked* by quadrature for every $(l, i)$ below.

### Projectors in reciprocal space

With the plane waves of 1a, $|\mathbf{q}\rangle = \Omega^{-1/2}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$
and $\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}$, the Rayleigh expansion gives for a
projector centred on an atom at $\boldsymbol\tau$

$$
\big\langle p_i^l Y_{lm};\boldsymbol\tau\,\big|\,\mathbf{q}\big\rangle
= \Omega^{-1/2}\, e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau}\; i^{\,l}\;
Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})\;\hat p_i^l(q),
\qquad
\hat p_i^l(q) = 4\pi\int_0^\infty p_i^l(r)\,j_l(qr)\,r^2\,dr .
$$

The radial transforms are analytic [@hgh1998]. With $y = (q r_l)^2$:

| $l$ | $i$ | $\hat p_i^l(q)\,\big/\,\big(\pi^{5/4}\,e^{-y/2}\big)$ |
|:--:|:--:|:--|
| 0 | 1 | $4\sqrt2\; r_l^{3/2}$ |
| 0 | 2 | $8\sqrt{2/15}\; r_l^{3/2}\,(3 - y)$ |
| 0 | 3 | $\tfrac{16}{3}\sqrt{2/105}\; r_l^{3/2}\,(15 - 10y + y^2)$ |
| 1 | 1 | $\tfrac{8}{\sqrt3}\; r_l^{5/2}\,q$ |
| 1 | 2 | $\tfrac{16}{\sqrt{105}}\; r_l^{5/2}\,q\,(5 - y)$ |
| 1 | 3 | $\tfrac{32}{3\sqrt{1155}}\; r_l^{5/2}\,q\,(35 - 14y + y^2)$ |
| 2 | 1 | $8\sqrt{2/15}\; r_l^{7/2}\,q^2$ |
| 2 | 2 | $\tfrac{16}{3}\sqrt{2/105}\; r_l^{7/2}\,q^2\,(7 - y)$ |

*Checked* against numerical quadrature of the defining integral at
$q = 0.3, 1, 3, 7$ Bohr⁻¹ for all eight entries: the worst relative
difference was $5\times10^{-14}$ ($3\times10^{-15}$ in the review). These are
cell-independent, in Bohr$^{3/2}$; the reduced form $\hat p_i^l(q)/q^l$ used
by the protocol below carries Bohr$^{3/2+l}$.
[@hgh1998] quotes them with the factor $\Omega^{-1/2}$ included; we keep that
factor outside, for the same reason the local form factor is kept free of
$1/\Omega$: the pseudopotential object must not know the cell. Silicon needs
only the first two $s$ rows and the first $p$ row. The others are listed so
that the parser and the tests cover the general table up to $l = 2$; higher
$l$ and $i$ are refused until an element needs them.

### Matrix elements and the operator

Summing over atoms $a$ with per-atom weights $\lambda_a$, the phases
$e^{\pm i\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau}$ cancel between bra and ket, and so
do the factors $i^{\,l}$, because $h$ is diagonal in $l$ and no cross-$l$
terms exist:

$$
\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}|V_\text{nl}|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}'\rangle
= \frac1\Omega\sum_a \lambda_a\, e^{-i(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_a}
\sum_{l}\sum_{i,j}\hat p_i^l(q)\,h_{ij}^l\,\hat p_j^l(q')
\sum_m Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})\,Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}}') ,
$$

and by the addition theorem $\sum_m Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}}')
= \tfrac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(\hat{\mathbf{q}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{q}}')$. The sum over
$m$ is therefore the same for any real orthonormal basis of the
$(2l+1)$-dimensional shell: the real-harmonic convention and the ordering of
$m$ need not match DFTK's for the comparison to agree. The structure
factor sign is that of 1b. Unlike the local term, the matrix element depends
on $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}'$ separately, not on their
difference: that is what "nonlocal" means in reciprocal space, and why this
term cannot join the real-space effective potential.

The operator is never built as an $N_\text{PW}\times N_\text{PW}$ matrix. It
is the product

$$
V_\text{nl} = B\,D\,B^\dagger,
\qquad
B_{\mathbf{G},(a l m i)} = \Omega^{-1/2}\,e^{-i\mathbf{G}\cdot\boldsymbol\tau_a}\,
Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})\,\hat p_i^l(q),
\qquad
D_{(a l m i),(a' l' m' j)} = \lambda_a\,\delta_{aa'}\delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}\,h^l_{ij},
$$

with $B$ of shape $(N_\text{PW}, N_\text{proj})$, built once per k-point and
SCF run. Applying it to a block of bands costs
$O(N_\text{PW}N_\text{proj}N_\text{bands})$, with no FFT. Silicon has
$2 + 3\times1 = 5$ projectors per atom, so $N_\text{proj} = 10$ for the
primitive cell. *Checked:* the scratch operator, applied to the identity,
equals the Legendre formula above to $1.4\times10^{-16}$ Ha and is Hermitian
to $3\times10^{-17}$, on a geometry with no symmetry, at a general k-point and
with $\lambda = (1, 0.7)$.

This is an operator term in the sense of 1a (`prepare`/`apply`), next to the
kinetic term. Nothing in `apply_H`, the dense matrix, the eigensolvers or
the SCF changes. The weights scale $D$, so $V_\text{nl}$ is linear in
$\lambda_a$, as `CLAUDE.md` requires.

**The angular factor at $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} = 0$.** $Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})$
is undefined at $q = 0$ for $l > 0$, and its derivative with respect to the
cell or to $\mathbf{k}$ is singular there. But $\hat p_i^l(q) \propto q^l$
times a function of $q^2$, and $q^l\,Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})$ is a
homogeneous polynomial in the Cartesian components of $\mathbf{q}$ (a solid
harmonic): $q\,Y_{1m} = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\,(q_x, q_y, q_z)$. The other factor,
$\hat p_i^l(q)/q^l$, is by the table above a polynomial in $y = q^2r_l^2$
times $e^{-y/2}$. The whole matrix element is thus a polynomial in
$q_x, q_y, q_z$ times a Gaussian, with no square root anywhere. **Rule:** the
implementation evaluates the product
$\big[q^lY_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf{q}})\big]\cdot\big[\hat p_i^l(q)/q^l\big]$, the
first factor from the Cartesian components of $\mathbf{q}$ and the second
from $q^2$. It never forms $\hat{\mathbf{q}}$ and never forms $q$. Then the
$\Gamma$ point needs no special case and derivatives of every order are
finite. This differs from the local term of 2a, where `local(q)` takes the
magnitude and needs a double-`where` guard around the square root. A guarded
square root would also give correct first derivatives here, but only
because $\nabla q^2 = 0$ where $q = 0$, and it would fail for the second
derivatives that phonons will need. The review pointed this out.

### Energy and derivatives

The nonlocal energy is the expectation value of the operator,

$$
E_\text{nl} = \sum_\mathbf{k} w_\mathbf{k}\sum_n f_{n\mathbf{k}}\,
\langle\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}|V_\text{nl}|\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}\rangle
= \sum_\mathbf{k} w_\mathbf{k}\sum_n f_{n\mathbf{k}}\;
\big(B^\dagger c_{n\mathbf{k}}\big)^\dagger D\,\big(B^\dagger c_{n\mathbf{k}}\big),
$$

added to the direct functional of 2a exactly as the kinetic energy is. It is
not a functional of the density, so it has no potential on the grid and does
not enter `total_potential`. In the double-counting form it is already inside
the band sum $\sum w f\varepsilon$, so that form is unchanged.

The explicit dependence on the structure is in $B$ (positions through the
phase, the cell through $q$, $\hat{\mathbf{q}}$ and $\Omega^{-1/2}$) and $D$
(weights). The Hellmann–Feynman argument of 2a carries over unchanged: the
orbitals are stopped, and `jax.grad` of the direct energy gives the force
including the nonlocal contribution. There is no separately coded nonlocal
force. A translation of all atoms multiplies $B$ by a phase that cancels in
$BDB^\dagger$ up to a unitary transformation of the orbitals, so the nonlocal
term is exactly translation-covariant and adds nothing to the egg-box effect.

### Silicon parameters and the protocol

The HGH LDA parameters for silicon [@hgh1998], as distributed in DFTK's
PseudoLibrary (`hgh_lda_hgh/si-q4.hgh`) [@pseudolibrary_si], are

| | | |
|:--|:--|:--|
| local | $Z = 4$, $r_\text{loc} = 0.44$ Bohr | $C_1 = -7.33610297$ Ha |
| $s$ ($l = 0$) | $r_s = 0.42273813$ Bohr | $h^s_{11} = 5.90692831$, $h^s_{12} = -1.26189397$, $h^s_{22} = 3.25819622$ Ha |
| $p$ ($l = 1$) | $r_p = 0.48427842$ Bohr | $h^p_{11} = 2.72701346$ Ha |

The file stores the upper triangle of each $h^l$. In [@hgh1998] the
off-diagonal elements are fixed by the diagonal ones;
$h^s_{12} = -\tfrac12\sqrt{3/5}\,h^s_{22}$ reproduces the stored value to all
digits, which is a check of the reading of the format. The file has no
spin–orbit coefficients. As for hydrogen, the parameters are in atomic units
and are stored verbatim, with the file hash pinned.

Two derived constants fix conventions sharply, where hydrogen could not:

- $\alpha(\mathrm{Si}) = 2\pi Z r_\text{loc}^2 + (2\pi)^{3/2}r_\text{loc}^3C_1
  = -4.976\,525$ Ha·Bohr³.
- At $a = 10.263$ Bohr ($\Omega = 270.248$ Bohr³) the eigenvalue shift
  $\sum_j\alpha_j/\Omega$ is $-0.036\,829$ Ha, and the $\mathbf{G}=0$ energy
  $N_\text{el}\sum_j\alpha_j/\Omega$ is $-0.294\,634$ Ha. In 2a these were
  $10^{-6}$ Ha and nearly invisible. Here a wrong $\mathbf{G}=0$ convention is
  a 1 eV error in the eigenvalues and 0.3 Ha in the energy.

The same caveat as in 2a applies to the functional: the parameters were
fitted with the Padé LDA and are used with PW92.

**Ghost states.** A separable pseudopotential is not equivalent to the
semilocal one it was derived from, except on the atomic reference states.
Away from them it can support spurious, deeply bound *ghost* states below
the physical valence levels. The usual cause in the Kleinman–Bylander
construction is a poor choice of the local channel. HGH has an analytic
local part rather than a chosen channel, and its silicon parameters are
known to be free of ghosts, but the failure mode exists in general and is
cheap to test for. The lowest eigenvalue at every k-point of the grid must
belong to the $3s$-derived band: in the review the lowest level is Γ₁ at
$-11.98$ eV below the valence-band maximum, with nothing below it. The same
assert would catch a mis-signed $h^l$ or a mis-parsed projector block.

**Protocol.** The pseudopotential object gains its nonlocal radial data, in
the spirit of `local(q)`: for each channel, $l$, the coupling matrix $h^l$
(Ha) and the reduced projectors $\hat p_i^l(q)/q^l$ as traceable functions of
$q^2$, not of $q$ (cell-independent, Bohr$^{3/2+l}$). A pseudopotential without projectors exposes no
channels, and the nonlocal term is then zero; hydrogen and Cohen–Bergstresser
are unchanged. The nonlocal Hamiltonian term reads only this interface, and
only the parser reads the file. The exact signatures are agreed in the
engineering log before implementation, as for earlier milestones.

## Brillouin-zone sampling

In a crystal the Kohn–Sham orbitals are labelled by a wavevector
$\mathbf{k}$ in the Brillouin zone, and the density and every energy are
averages over it, approximated by a sum over a uniform grid
[@monkhorst_pack1976]:

$$
\frac{1}{\Omega_\text{BZ}}\int_\text{BZ} g(\mathbf{k})\,d\mathbf{k}
\;\approx\; \sum_{\mathbf{k}} w_\mathbf{k}\,g(\mathbf{k}),
\qquad
\mathbf{k} = \sum_{i=1}^{3}\frac{n_i + s_i}{N_i}\,\mathbf{b}_i,
\quad n_i = 0,\dots,N_i-1,\quad w_\mathbf{k} = \frac{1}{N_1N_2N_3}.
$$

For an insulator this sum converges exponentially with the grid density.
The grid sum is the periodic trapezoid rule, whose error is the set of
Fourier coefficients of $g$ at the aliasing vectors, and those decay
exponentially when $g$ is analytic in $\mathbf{k}$. Individual band energies
are *not* analytic: bands are degenerate at symmetry points and cross inside
the valence manifold, so each $\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$ has kinks. What is
analytic is the projector onto the occupied manifold, and with it
$\sum_{n\le4}\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$ and $\rho_\mathbf{k}$, which are what
the energy and the density are built from. It is analytic because the gap
does not close, and that is the only place the insulating condition enters.

The 2a formulas for $\rho$, $E_\text{kin}$ and the band sum already carry
$\mathbf{k}$ and $w_\mathbf{k}$. What 2b adds is the grid, the weights as an
input of the SCF, and the points below where "per k-point" and "over all
k-points" differ.

**Equivalence to a supercell.** The unshifted $N\times N\times N$ grid is
exactly the set of wavevectors compatible with periodic boundary conditions
on a supercell of $N^3$ primitive cells. This gives an independent meaning to
a k-grid calculation and an analytic rung for the tests: a $\Gamma$-only
calculation in a supercell and an $N$-grid calculation in the primitive cell
describe the same electrons.

### The grid is unshifted, and why

Three choices are made here, each with a consequence for the invariants.

- **$\Gamma$-centred ($s_i = 0$).** The unshifted grid is the reciprocal
  lattice of the supercell lattice, so it is mapped onto itself by every
  point-group operation of the crystal. The discrete problem then has the
  full symmetry of the structure, and "the SCF solution preserves the
  symmetry of the input structure" (`CLAUDE.md`) holds without symmetrising
  anything. A half-shifted grid does not have this property, and the price
  of avoiding it is slower convergence with $N$; both are quantified below
  the list.
- **No symmetry reduction.** The full grid is used with uniform weights. The
  SCF nevertheless takes $w_\mathbf{k}$ as an input and assumes nothing about
  it except $\sum w_\mathbf{k} = 1$, so an irreducible wedge with unequal
  weights and a symmetrised density can be added later without touching the
  SCF. Time-reversal ($\varepsilon_{n,-\mathbf{k}} = \varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$,
  $\psi_{n,-\mathbf{k}} = \overline{\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}}$) would halve the work.
  It is exactly free, because
  $\rho_{-\mathbf{k}} = \overline{\rho_\mathbf{k}} = \rho_\mathbf{k}$: folding
  $\mathbf{k}$ with $-\mathbf{k}$ changes nothing in the density, and the
  review reproduced the unfolded energy bit for bit from the folded $2^3$
  grid. It is a pure factor of two with no physics attached, so it is
  deferred to a milestone where cost matters. Until then it is a test: the
  eigenvalues at $\mathbf{k}$ and $-\mathbf{k}$ on the grid must agree.
- **Fractional coordinates in $[0, 1)$.** DFTK lists the same grid in
  $[-\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$. The two differ by reciprocal lattice vectors, and
  the basis $\{\mathbf{G}: \tfrac12|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}|^2 \le E_\text{cut}\}$
  at $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}_0$ is the basis at $\mathbf{k}$ relabelled, so the
  discrete problems are identical. That invariance is itself a test.

k-points remain a batch dimension: one `vmap` over the grid, as since 1a.
The density on the FFT grid has no k index, so the SCF state and the mixer
are unchanged.

**What a shifted grid breaks, and what the unshifted grid costs.** Shifted
Monkhorst–Pack grids are the standard choice for fcc, so the choice above
needs its reason stated. The review decomposed the grids into stars, the
sets of k-points related by the 48 cubic operations:

| grid | stars touched | members present / full star size |
|:--|:--:|:--|
| unshifted $2^3$ | 3 | 1/1, 4/4, 3/3 |
| unshifted $4^3$ | 8 | all members of every star |
| half-shifted $2^3$ | 2 | 2/8, 6/24 |
| half-shifted $4^3$ | 10 | one quarter of every star |

The shifted grid is not closed under the cubic group, but it contains the
*same fraction* of every star it touches. A uniform-weight sum over it of
any quantity that is invariant under the point group therefore equals the
fully symmetric star-weighted average exactly. That is why the shifted
$2^3$ grid reduces to the two special points of Chadi and Cohen
[@chadi_cohen1973] with weights $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac34$, and why band
energies and eigenvalue sums are symmetry-correct on a shifted grid. The
density is different: $\rho_{R\mathbf{k}}$ is a rotated copy of
$\rho_\mathbf{k}$, not equal to it, so $\sum_\mathbf{k}w_\mathbf{k}\rho_\mathbf{k}$
is symmetric only if the grid contains every member of each star. A code
that does not symmetrise the density converges to a slightly asymmetric
$\rho$ on a shifted grid. Forces that should vanish are the sharpest
symptom: at the ideal geometry with $E_\text{cut} = 12$ Ha, the largest force
component is $8\times10^{-16}$ Ha/Bohr on the unshifted $2^3$ grid and
$1.0\times10^{-3}$ Ha/Bohr on the $2^3$ grid shifted by
$(\tfrac14,\tfrac14,\tfrac14)$ (throwaway check, confirmed by the review).
DFTK can use shifted grids because it symmetrises the density; jaxdft in 2b
does not, so it must use the Γ-centred grid.

The price, from the review, at $E_\text{cut} = 15$ Ha:

| grid | k-points | $E$ (Ha) | $E - E(\text{unshifted }6^3)$ (mHa) |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| unshifted $2^3$ | 8 | −7.838092 | 95.0 |
| half-shifted $2^3$ | 8 | −7.927201 | 5.9 |
| unshifted $4^3$ | 64 | −7.926852 | 6.3 |
| half-shifted $3^3$ | 27 | −7.933259 | −0.1 |
| unshifted $6^3$ | 216 | −7.933125 | 0 |

A half-shifted grid matches the unshifted grid of twice the linear size, at
an eighth of the k-points. That is what the symmetry choice costs, and it is
large enough that a shifted grid with density symmetrisation is a natural
candidate for a later milestone.

**The FFT grid at $\mathbf{k} \ne 0$.** The aliasing argument of 2a does not
depend on $\mathbf{k}$: two basis vectors at the same $\mathbf{k}$ differ by
at most $2G_\text{max}$, so the grid rule carries over unchanged. The
placement of $\psi$ on the grid does depend on it. The sphere around
$-\mathbf{k}$ reaches $|\mathbf{G}| \le G_\text{max} + |\mathbf{k}|$, so the
largest Miller index grows with the k-grid, and it must stay below $N_i/2$
or two basis functions share a grid frequency. It holds with room here
(from the review: $\max|m_i| = 6$ against $N/2 = 12$ at 12 Ha, and 11
against 22.5 at 40 Ha), and the basis enumeration already includes the
largest $|\mathbf{k}|$ in its bound. The basis asserts the inequality.

### Occupations, the gap and the frontier over all k-points

Silicon has $N_\text{el} = 8$ per cell: four doubly occupied valence bands at
every k-point, $f_{n\mathbf{k}} = 2$ for $n \le 4$. That is the aufbau filling
of the whole crystal **only if the system is gapped over the grid**:

$$
\varepsilon_\text{VBM} = \max_\mathbf{k}\varepsilon_{4\mathbf{k}}
\;<\;
\varepsilon_\text{CBM} = \min_\mathbf{k}\varepsilon_{5\mathbf{k}} .
$$

In an indirect-gap material these are at different k-points, so a positive
gap at every k-point separately does not imply it. The 2a guard compares
band $N_\text{el}/2 + 1$ with band $N_\text{el}/2$ per k-point. Run on a
local-only silicon-like potential, which is a semimetal, it accepted a
"converged" state with $\varepsilon_\text{CBM} - \varepsilon_\text{VBM} = -0.03$ Ha.
The review confirmed the behaviour at $E_\text{cut} = 12$ Ha on the $2^3$
grid: a gap over the grid of $-0.063$ Ha while the smallest per-k gap was
$+0.0001$ Ha. **Rule:** the guard is on the gap over all k-points of the grid,
$\varepsilon_\text{CBM} - \varepsilon_\text{VBM} > $ `min_gap`. It is still a
numerical criterion: it says the fixed occupations are the ground-state
occupations of this discrete problem, not that the material is an insulator
at a finer grid.

The guard is evaluated **at convergence**, as the acceptance criterion of
the result. During the SCF the fixed occupations can be non-aufbau for
several iterations even when the converged state is gapped (the initial
Gaussian density has a much smaller gap), so a guard applied to every
iterate would reject healthy runs. The gap over the grid is recorded in the
SCF history at every iteration, so that a closing gap is visible before the
run ends.

**Fractional electron counts and the weight derivatives.** With per-atom
weights, $N_\text{el} = \sum_j\lambda_jZ_j$ need not be an even integer.
Extra charge then goes into the lowest empty states *of the crystal*, and
missing charge comes out of the highest occupied ones. Janak's theorem over
the grid reads $\partial E/\partial f_{n\mathbf{k}} = w_\mathbf{k}\,\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$,
so the one-sided derivatives of 2a become

$$
\frac{\partial E}{\partial\lambda_j}\bigg|_\pm
= \frac{\partial E_\text{direct}}{\partial\lambda_j}\bigg|_{\psi,f\ \text{fixed}} + Z_j\,\varepsilon_\pm,
\qquad
\varepsilon_- = \varepsilon_\text{VBM},\quad \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_\text{CBM},
$$

with the frontier levels taken over all k-points, and the two sides differ
by $Z_j$ times the gap over the grid. The explicit term now includes
$\partial E_\text{nl}/\partial\lambda_j$. The 2a implementation gives every
k-point the same occupations $f_n(N_\text{el})$, so at more than one k-point
it returns $Z_j\sum_\mathbf{k}w_\mathbf{k}\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$, the
Brillouin-zone *average* of a band rather than its edge. In the throwaway
check on a displaced geometry with a $3^3$ grid, the two sides differed by
$Z\times0.112$ Ha, while the gap over the grid was 0.010 Ha (the review
reproduced both: 0.1122 and 0.0103 Ha). That is a wrong derivative, not a
convention, and 2b must replace it. The structural identity alone detects
it, with no fractional-charge SCF.

The frontier level is generally degenerate: the valence-band maximum at
$\Gamma$ is a triplet, the conduction minimum on a $\Gamma$-centred grid is
shared by symmetry-equivalent k-points, and time reversal pairs $\mathbf{k}$
with $-\mathbf{k}$ even when all spatial symmetry is broken. **Rule:** charge
added or removed is shared equally among all states $(n,\mathbf{k})$ within a
tolerance of the frontier level, so that
$\sum_{\text{frontier}} w_\mathbf{k}\,df_{n\mathbf{k}} = dN_\text{el}$. To first
order the energy change does not depend on how the charge is shared, since
all those states have the same eigenvalue. Sharing equally keeps the density
symmetric, in line with the preference of `CLAUDE.md` for quantities
invariant within degenerate subspaces.

2b implements these occupations and tests both sides against finite
differences of fractional-charge SCF runs
([decision 1](#decisions-from-review)). Two points from the review keep
that test well-posed. The frontier is at least two-fold degenerate whenever
its k-point is not time-reversal invariant, so the main test uses a
geometry and grid whose frontier sits at a time-reversal-invariant point
of the grid, where the level is non-degenerate and the sharing rule is not
exercised; a degenerate frontier is a separate, looser test. And because
the frontier set is defined by a tolerance, $E(\lambda)$ is only piecewise
smooth: the finite difference is one-sided, with $\delta$ small enough that
the frontier set is the same at $\lambda$ and $\lambda \mp \delta$, and the
test asserts that the two sets are equal.

### Bands, buffer bands and the eigensolver

The SCF needs the four valence bands at every k-point, and the lowest
conduction band for the gap guard and the right-hand derivative. Levels in
silicon are degenerate at symmetric k-points (a triplet at the top of the
valence band at $\Gamma$, another just above the gap), so a fixed number of
bands can cut through a degenerate level. The density is unaffected, because
only complete levels are occupied, but the last eigenvector is then
ill-conditioned and LOBPCG converges it slowly. From the throwaway check
($E_\text{cut} = 15$ Ha, $4^3$ grid), asking for 5 bands took 535 eigensolver
iterations in total over the SCF, and 8 bands took 424, with total energies
equal to $10^{-14}$ Ha.

Iterations are not the cost, though. Each band in the block costs a pair of
FFTs per iteration, so the cost is iterations times block width. The review
counted band-applications over a full SCF at the same size, with LOBPCG at
the same tolerance:

| bands requested | band-applications | SCF steps | $E$ (Ha) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 5 | 37 036 | 11 | −7.926851643 |
| 6 | 43 467 | 11 | −7.926851643 |
| 8 | 64 571 | 11 | −7.926851643 |
| 10 | 67 026 | 11 | −7.926851644 |

Iterations per band fall with buffer bands, as in the throwaway check, but
the total work rises by 74 % from 5 to 8 bands for the same energy. On a
GPU a wider block is cheaper per column, so the balance can go the other
way. Whether buffer bands pay is a wall-clock question on the target
device, and the two iteration counts above do not answer it.

**Rule:** convergence is required, and asserted, only for the bands the SCF
needs ($N_\text{el}/2 + 1$). The eigensolver may carry *buffer* bands above
them, which speed up the convergence of the ones below and are otherwise
ignored. Their number is a setting, not a physical requirement, with a
default of one, to be revisited by wall-clock measurement on the GPU
([decision 2](#decisions-from-review)). The result must not depend on it.

**Bands from the converged density.** The band structure along a path is
*not* self-consistent: the density $\rho^\ast$ from the grid SCF is fixed,
and $H[\rho^\ast](\mathbf{k})$ is diagonalised at arbitrary $\mathbf{k}$. The
diagonalisation step is exact, not an approximation: the Kohn–Sham
Hamiltonian depends on the orbitals only through $\rho$, so its eigenvalues
at any $\mathbf{k}$ are those of the same converged potential. But
$\rho^\ast$ is the density of the discrete k-grid problem, and the bands
inherit its k-grid error (about 0.02 eV on the $4^3$ grid; see the band
table below). The path needs more bands than the SCF: the L₃ and X₁
conduction levels quoted below require eight to ten, not five.
`band_structure` already accepts a
fixed density, and the FFT grid depends only on the cell and the cutoff, so
a path basis and the SCF basis share one grid. A consistency test follows:
at a k-point that is on the SCF grid, the band-structure eigenvalues must
equal the SCF eigenvalues.

## The SCF for a bulk semiconductor

The fixed-point formulation is unchanged. Three remarks on why the 2a
choices are expected to carry over:

- **Mixing.** Charge sloshing grows with the cell size and with the
  dielectric response at long wavelength. The primitive cell of a
  semiconductor has neither problem: the smallest nonzero $|\mathbf{G}|$ is
  large, and the screening is finite. The throwaway check converged to
  $\|F(\rho)-\rho\| < 10^{-9}$ in 9 or 10 Anderson steps at every cutoff and
  grid tried, and the review's Pulay mixer in 10 to 12 with no stalls. No
  Kerker preconditioning in 2b.
- **Initial density.** Atomic Gaussians of width 0.8 Bohr, as in 2a, were
  adequate. The converged result must not depend on them.
- **Vacuum.** There is none: the density is bounded away from zero, so
  clip-then-renormalise should never act on a converged run. The SCF history
  records the change it makes at each iterate, and the test asserts that it
  is zero at convergence.

**Grid symmetry.** The point-group operations of the fcc lattice are integer
matrices in fractional coordinates, so they map an $N\times N\times N$ grid
onto itself. Diamond is nonsymmorphic: with the origin at the bond centre
(the 1b convention), inversion is a pure point operation, but the operations
of the tetrahedral site group carry fractional translations. For a
tetrahedral operation $R$ about the atom at $\boldsymbol\tau$ the translation
is $\boldsymbol\tau - R\boldsymbol\tau$; for the twofold rotation about $x$
it is $\tfrac{a}{4}(0,1,1) = \tfrac12\mathbf{a}_1$. The review enumerated the
whole space group: 48 operations, with translations $(0,0,0)$,
$(\tfrac12,0,0)$, $(0,\tfrac12,0)$ and $(0,0,\tfrac12)$ in the primitive
fractional basis, 12 operations each. These are *halves* of primitive
lattice vectors. (In cubic fractional coordinates the same vectors have
components of $\tfrac14$, which is where the draft of this post went wrong
and required $4 \mid N$.) The FFT grid is laid out along the primitive
vectors, so the operations map the grid onto itself if and only if **$N$ is
even in every direction**. Since XC is evaluated on the grid, the discrete
problem has the full symmetry of the crystal only then. At the ideal
geometry, where every force should vanish:

| $E_\text{cut}$ (Ha) | grid $N$ | $N$ even | operations mapping the grid onto itself | largest force (Ha/Bohr) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 12 | 24 | yes | 48/48 | $8\times10^{-16}$ |
| 12 | 25 | no | 12/48 | $6\times10^{-7}$ |
| 12 | 26 | yes | 48/48 | $2\times10^{-15}$ |
| 15 | 25 | no | 12/48 | $1\times10^{-7}$ |
| 15 | 26 | yes | 48/48 | $5\times10^{-15}$ |
| 15 | 28 | yes | 48/48 | $1\times10^{-15}$ |

The $N = 24$, 25 and 28 rows are from the throwaway check and were
reproduced by the review; the $N = 26$ rows and the operation counts are
from the review. $N = 26$ is the discriminating case: even, not a multiple
of 4, and symmetric to machine precision.

The net force vanishes on every grid (to $10^{-15}$ Ha/Bohr), because
inversion about the origin always maps the grid onto itself. This is the
egg-box effect of 2a in another guise, and it is larger here than for H₂:
translating the crystal rigidly by half a grid spacing at
$E_\text{cut} = 12$ Ha changed the energy by $2.0\times10^{-7}$ Ha, against
$2\times10^{-11}$ Ha for H₂ at its test size, while a translation by a whole
grid spacing changed it by $2\times10^{-15}$ Ha. Presumably the silicon
density has more weight at large $|\mathbf{G}|$ relative to the grid than
the H₂ density had; this was not measured. The mechanism is indirect, since
the XC energy has no explicit dependence on the positions. The XC
quadrature is the only term that is not exactly translation-covariant, so
it is the only term that lets the self-consistent density break the
symmetry. The asymmetric density then produces a force through the terms
that do depend on the positions ($E_\text{loc}$, $E_\text{nl}$,
$E_\text{Ewald}$). Switching XC off tests that chain (see the forces below).

Consequences: symmetry tests are exact (tolerance $10^{-10}$) on grids with
even $N$ and hold only to the egg-box level otherwise, and the test size
uses an even grid. The default grid rule is *not* changed, since the
residual is small and the rule is shared with DFTK. It already returns an
even $N$ whenever it rounds an odd bound up to an even FFT-friendly size
(23 → 24 at 12 Ha, 29 → 30 at 20 Ha), and an odd $N$ only when the bound is
itself FFT-friendly (25 at 15 Ha). The basis gains an option that rounds up
to a size compatible with given fractional translations
([decision 3](#decisions-from-review)).

## Forces and the cell

**Forces.** Diamond silicon at equilibrium has no forces, so the
finite-difference test displaces one atom in a general direction. From the
throwaway check ($E_\text{cut} = 12$ Ha, $3^3$ grid, atom 1 displaced by
$(0.012, -0.005, 0.008)$ in fractional coordinates), the autodiff derivative
$\partial E/\partial f_{1x} = 0.102\,076\,953$ Ha differs from a central
difference by $1.02\times10^{-6}$ at step $h = 2\times10^{-3}$ and
$2.55\times10^{-7}$ at $h = 10^{-3}$: a clean $h^2$, with the nonlocal term
included. The two atoms' derivatives sum to about $4\times10^{-6}$ Ha per unit
fractional coordinate, i.e. a net force of about $5\times10^{-7}$ Ha/Bohr.
That is the egg-box effect above (the displaced geometry has no inversion
centre on the grid), not an error in a term: on the $2^3$ grid the same
geometry has a net force of $5.7\times10^{-7}$ Ha/Bohr with XC and
$4\times10^{-15}$ Ha/Bohr with the XC term removed. That pair is an
acceptance test.

**The cell, and what $E(a)$ means.** At a fixed set of Miller indices the
energy is a smooth function of the lattice vectors, and its autodiff
derivative must agree with finite differences at that fixed basis, now
including the nonlocal term (whose projectors depend on the cell through
$q$ and $\Omega^{-1/2}$). As in 2a that derivative is the stress of a
*fixed-basis* calculation. It is not the slope of the energy–volume curve at
fixed cutoff: stretching the cell at fixed Miller indices lowers the
effective cutoff, and the difference is the Pulay stress, of the order of
the cutoff error of the energy divided by the volume. 2b therefore obtains
the lattice constant from separate SCF runs at fixed $E_\text{cut}$, each with
its own basis, and reports the autodiff cell derivative only as a tested
derivative. Because the basis changes discontinuously with $a$ at fixed
cutoff, $E(a)$ is not perfectly smooth; the jumps are bounded by the cutoff
error, which is why the curve is computed at a well-converged cutoff.

## What the results should look like

All numbers in this section are from the throwaway check: HGH silicon,
Slater + PW92, $a = 10.263$ Bohr (the experimental 5.431 Å) unless stated,
$\Gamma$-centred grids, the default FFT grid, $\tau_\text{SCF} = 10^{-9}$.

**Convergence of the total energy** (Ha per primitive cell):

| $E_\text{cut}$ (Ha), $4^3$ grid | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 30 | 40 |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $N_\text{PW}$ (largest k) | 150 | 415 | 754 | 1174 | 2148 | 3287 |
| $E$ | −7.86914 | −7.92143 | −7.92685 | −7.92747 | −7.92770 | −7.92772 |
| $E - E(40)$ (mHa) | 58.6 | 6.30 | 0.87 | 0.25 | 0.03 | 0 |

| $N^3$ grid, $E_\text{cut} = 15$ Ha | $1^3$ | $2^3$ | $3^3$ | $4^3$ | $5^3$ | $6^3$ |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| $E$ | −7.30090 | −7.83809 | −7.91059 | −7.92685 | −7.93157 | −7.93312 |
| $E - E(6^3)$ (mHa) | 632 | 95.0 | 22.5 | 6.3 | 1.6 | 0 |

- HGH silicon is a **soft** pseudopotential, unlike HGH hydrogen: 1 mHa at
  15 Ha, against 80 Ha for comparable convergence of H₂. The energy decreases
  monotonically with the cutoff. It must do so at a fixed FFT grid. The
  table uses the default grid, which changes at every column ($N = 15$, 24,
  25, 30, 36, 45), and changing the grid at a fixed cutoff is not
  variational: from the review, $E = -7.836151895$, $-7.836151704$ and
  $-7.836151623$ Ha on $N = 24$, 25, 26 at 12 Ha, a spread of
  $2.7\times10^{-7}$ Ha with the largest grid highest. That is a hundred
  times smaller than the smallest step in the table, so the monotonicity
  seen here is safe, but the assert holds the grid fixed.
- The k-grid, not the cutoff, limits the accuracy. The error falls by a
  factor of about 4 per step in $N$, consistent with exponential convergence
  for an insulator, but from a large prefactor: the unshifted grid is the
  slowest-converging uniform grid. The half-shifted $3^3$ grid of the review
  lies 0.13 mHa *below* the $6^3$ value, so $6^3$ is within about 0.2 mHa of
  the limit. Convergence with $N$ is **not variational** and need not be
  monotone in general, though it is here. $\Gamma$ alone is useless (0.6 Ha
  off).
- At $E_\text{cut} = 15$ Ha on the $4^3$ grid, the terms are
  $E_\text{kin} = 3.1728$, $E_\text{nl} = 1.5855$, $E_\text{loc} = -2.4435$,
  $E_\text{H} = 0.5590$, $E_\text{xc} = -2.4027$ and $E_\text{Ewald} = -8.3980$ Ha.
  The nonlocal energy is positive and large: the projectors are repulsive,
  standing in for the orthogonality to the core states.

**Kohn–Sham bands** from the converged density ($E_\text{cut} = 15$ Ha, $4^3$
grid), in eV from the valence-band maximum, with the published
Cohen–Bergstresser values (Table I of [@cb1966], not the converged
reproduction of 1b) for comparison. The third column, from the review, uses
the density of the $6^3$ grid instead:

| Level or splitting | LDA, $4^3$ density | LDA, $6^3$ density | CB published [@cb1966] |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| Γ₁ (valence-band width) | −11.98 | −11.97 | — |
| Γ₂₅′ – Γ₁₅ | 2.54 | 2.55 | 3.4 |
| Γ₂₅′ – Γ₂′ | 3.12 | 3.12 | 3.8 |
| Γ₂₅′ – L₁ | 1.41 | 1.42 | 1.9 |
| indirect gap (Δ₁ minimum) | 0.47, at 0.85 of Γ–X | 0.50, at 0.84 of Γ–X | 0.8 |
| conduction level at X | 0.61 | 0.63 | — |
| L₃′ – L₁ | 2.61 | | 3.1 |
| L₃′ – L₃ | 4.51 | | 5.2 |
| X₄ – X₁ | 3.47 | | 4.0 |

- The bands carry about 0.02 eV of k-grid error through the density. That
  is negligible against the differences from Cohen–Bergstresser, and the
  denser grid moves the indirect gap towards the published LDA value quoted
  below.
- The degeneracies are those of 1b: 1, 3, 3, 1 at Γ; pairs at X; 1, 1, 2, 1,
  2 at L. They are structural checks that need no reference.
- **Every gap is smaller than Cohen–Bergstresser's, by 0.3 to 0.9 eV.** This
  is the expected outcome and not a defect of the implementation. The
  Cohen–Bergstresser form factors were fitted to measured optical
  transitions. Kohn–Sham eigenvalue differences are not excitation energies:
  the LDA gap of silicon is about 0.5 eV against 1.17 eV in experiment, and
  the difference is a property of the Kohn–Sham construction and the
  functional, restored by quasiparticle corrections [@hybertsen_louie1986].
  The values above agree with the LDA values in that paper (indirect gap
  0.52 eV, Γ₂₅′–Γ₁₅ 2.57 eV) to within the differences expected between
  pseudopotentials.
- The **valence** bands should agree with Cohen–Bergstresser much better
  than the conduction bands, and the validation document quantifies that
  along the 1b path. The conduction-band minimum is in the same place, at
  about 0.85 of Γ–X.
- The indirect gap on the SCF k-grid is not the indirect gap: the $4^3$ grid
  contains X but not the Δ minimum, so the grid gap is 0.61 eV. The gap
  guard uses the former; the reported gap comes from the band-structure
  search along Δ, as in 1b.
- Eigenvalues carry the $\alpha$ shift of $-0.0368$ Ha and the
  average-potential convention of 2a. Only differences are physical.

**Lattice constant.** Total-energy calculations in the LDA have reproduced
the lattice constant and bulk modulus of silicon to about a per cent and a
few per cent since [@yin_cohen1982]. The sign of the deviation depends on
the correlation parametrisation and the pseudopotential, so no sign is
claimed here beyond the one measured. From the throwaway check at $E_\text{cut} = 20$ Ha on the $4^3$
grid, a cubic fit to seven energies between 9.9 and 10.5 Bohr gives
$a_0 = 10.193$ Bohr (5.394 Å, 0.7 % below the experimental 5.431 Å) and
$B_0 = 97$ GPa (experiment: about 99 GPa). The $4^3$ grid is not converged
(table above), so the validation document repeats this on a denser grid and
reports how far $a_0$ moves.

None of these numbers is an acceptance value.

## Invariants and checks

Everything listed in 2a continues to hold and is not repeated. New in 2b:

**Nonlocal term**

- Projectors: $\int p_i^l(r)^2r^2dr = 1$, and $\hat p_i^l(q)$ against
  numerical quadrature, for every tabulated $(l, i)$.
- The parsed silicon file gives the parameters above;
  $h^s_{12} = -\tfrac12\sqrt{3/5}\,h^s_{22}$; $\alpha(\mathrm{Si}) = -4.976\,525$
  Ha·Bohr³. The hydrogen file still parses to a pseudopotential with no
  channels.
- The dense matrix of the operator equals the Legendre formula, at a general
  k-point, for a structure without symmetry and unequal weights.
- Hermitian; `apply_H` agrees with the dense matrix on random blocks
  (property test); padding stays decoupled.
- Linear in each $\lambda_a$; zero for an atom with $\lambda_a = 0$; zero for
  a pseudopotential without channels.
- Translating all atoms by $\mathbf{t}$ maps
  $V_\text{nl}(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}') \to e^{-i(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}')\cdot\mathbf{t}}V_\text{nl}(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}')$:
  the spectrum is unchanged to rounding, for any $\mathbf{t}$.
- Shifting $\mathbf{k}$ by a reciprocal lattice vector leaves the spectrum
  unchanged.
- Rank: the matrix has at most $N_\text{proj}$ nonzero eigenvalues.
- Finite value and finite derivatives with respect to cell, positions and
  $\mathbf{k}$ when the basis contains $\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} = 0$. This is
  the regression test for the square-root-free form.
- No ghost states: at every k-point of the grid the lowest eigenvalue
  belongs to the $3s$-derived band.
- $E_\text{nl}$ from the direct functional equals
  $\sum w f\langle\psi|V_\text{nl}|\psi\rangle$ evaluated with the dense matrix.

**k-point sampling**

- Weights sum to 1; the grid has $N_1N_2N_3$ distinct points; it is closed
  under $\mathbf{k}\to-\mathbf{k}$ and under the point group of the lattice,
  modulo reciprocal lattice vectors.
- $\int\rho = N_\text{el}$ for any weights summing to 1.
- The largest Miller index of every per-k basis is below $N_i/2$.
- Supercell equivalence, on a system small enough for the laptop: the energy
  per cell of a $\Gamma$-only calculation in a $2\times1\times1$ supercell
  equals that of a $2\times1\times1$ grid in the primitive cell. The FFT
  grids are passed explicitly, $(2N_1, N_2, N_3)$ against $(N_1, N_2, N_3)$;
  the two discrete problems are then identical, because the supercell Γ
  basis is the union of the primitive per-k bases at the same cutoff. The
  supercell problem also admits densities with only the supercell period,
  so the test starts from the symmetric atomic density and asserts, besides
  the energy, that the converged supercell density is invariant under the
  primitive translation. It runs first with XC switched off, where agreement
  is at solver tolerance, and then with XC
  ([decision 4](#decisions-from-review)).
- Empty-lattice rung: with no potential the grid energy of 1a's free
  electrons is the weighted sum of the analytic band energies.
- $\varepsilon_{n,-\mathbf{k}} = \varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}$ on the grid.
- The gap guard rejects a converged state whose gap over the grid is
  negative although every per-k gap is positive (the local-only silicon-like
  potential is the positive control). The SCF history records the gap over
  the grid at every iteration.

**SCF silicon** (test size below)

- Fixed point, $\int\rho = 8$, direct equals double-counting energy to
  $O(\tau_\text{SCF}^2)$, variational in the orbitals, monotone in
  $E_\text{cut}$ at a fixed grid and fixed k-grid.
- Independence of the initial density, mixing parameters and number of
  buffer bands. Iterative and dense eigensolvers agree.
- Clip-and-renormalise makes no change at convergence.
- On a grid with even $N$: the density is invariant under the operations
  of the diamond space group, forces at the ideal geometry vanish, and the
  degeneracies at Γ, X and L are exact, all to $10^{-10}$. This is asserted
  on $N = 24$ and on $N = 26$, which is not a multiple of 4. On an odd grid
  ($N = 25$): inversion and the net force are still exact, and the largest
  force is at the egg-box level, not zero.
- Band-structure eigenvalues at grid k-points equal the SCF eigenvalues.
- Level degeneracies at Γ, X and L as in 1b; the conduction minimum is
  interior to Γ–X.
- Exchanging the two atoms, or translating both by a grid vector, changes
  nothing.

**Derivatives**

- Forces against central finite differences at the displaced geometry.
- The net force at the displaced geometry is at the egg-box level, and at
  SCF accuracy with XC switched off.
- Cell gradient against finite differences at a fixed basis.
- One-sided $\partial E/\partial\lambda_j$: the two sides differ by $Z_j$
  times the gap over the grid. Each side against a one-sided finite
  difference of fractional-charge SCF runs, with the frontier set asserted
  equal at both ends of the step: once with a non-degenerate frontier at a
  time-reversal-invariant k-point, once (looser) with a degenerate one.

**Against references** (after implementation, as in 2a)

1. DFTK [@dftk2021] with `LDA()`, the same cell, cutoff, explicit `fft_size`
   and k-grid (`kshift` zero), `symmetries=false`, zero temperature, and the
   same pseudopotential file by hash. Compared: every energy term
   (`AtomicNonlocal` is new), the total, all eigenvalues of the needed bands
   at every k-point with the asserted shift of $+0.036\,829$ Ha, and forces
   at the displaced geometry. DFTK's `PspCorrection` must equal
   $-0.294\,634$ Ha. Script and outputs in `reference/dftk_si/`. According
   to the review, DFTK has its own notion of a symmetry-compatible grid
   (`symmetries_respect_rgrid`, `next_compatible_fft_size`), which is
   inactive when an explicit `fft_size` is given. With `symmetries=false`
   as well, it cannot affect the comparison; this is confirmed when the
   reference is run.
2. Published LDA band energies [@hybertsen_louie1986] and structural
   properties [@yin_cohen1982], in the validation document only: different
   pseudopotentials make them a plausibility check, not an acceptance value.
3. Cohen–Bergstresser (1b), in the validation document: a comparison of two
   models, with the differences interpreted as above.

### Test size

$a = 10.263$ Bohr, $E_\text{cut} = 12$ Ha (544 plane waves, a $24^3$ grid,
so $N$ is even) and the $2^3$ grid (8 k-points). The gap over that grid is
0.44 eV, so the state is gapped. A full SCF took 10 iterations and 6 s on
the laptop in the throwaway check, compilation included. The additions are
the displaced geometry of the force test, one run each on a $25^3$ and a
$26^3$ grid (the discriminating pair for grid symmetry), and the
$2\times1\times1$ supercell.

### Tolerances

- **Exact identities** (projector transforms, operator against the Legendre
  formula, Hermiticity, covariances, symmetry on an even grid, grid
  k-points against SCF eigenvalues): $10^{-10}$ in the relevant unit.
- **Symmetry on the odd grid** ($N = 25$, 12 Ha): the largest force at the
  ideal geometry is between $10^{-8}$ and $5\times10^{-6}$ Ha/Bohr (measured
  $6\times10^{-7}$). The lower bound makes it a control: the test fails if
  the odd grid is silently symmetric.
- **Monotonicity in $E_\text{cut}$:** asserted at a fixed FFT grid, with no
  tolerance beyond SCF accuracy.
- **SCF tolerance:** $\tau_\text{SCF} = 10^{-9}$, as in 2a.
- **Finite-difference forces:** fractional step $h = 10^{-3}$, tolerance
  $10^{-6}$ Ha per unit fractional coordinate (measured $2.6\times10^{-7}$,
  scaling as $h^2$).
- **Net force with XC:** below $5\times10^{-6}$ Ha/Bohr (measured
  $5.7\times10^{-7}$); without XC: below $10^{-8}$ Ha/Bohr (measured
  $4\times10^{-15}$; the bound is first order in $\tau_\text{SCF}$, since the
  net force vanishes only at self-consistency).
- **DFTK:** $10^{-7}$ Ha per energy term and in total, $10^{-6}$ Ha for
  eigenvalues, $10^{-6}$ Ha/Bohr for forces, as in 2a and for the same
  reason: both codes solve the same discrete problem.

## Decisions from review

The draft of this post ended with five open questions. The review answered
them, and these are the decisions taken. Where a decision goes beyond what
the review measured, that is said.

1. **Fractional electron counts at several k-points: implemented and tested
   in 2b.** Occupations with the frontier taken over all k-points and
   charge shared equally within a degenerate frontier level, and both
   one-sided weight derivatives compared with finite differences of
   fractional-charge SCF runs. A derivative never compared with a finite
   difference is an untested claim. The main test places the frontier at a
   time-reversal-invariant k-point, where it is non-degenerate; a degenerate
   frontier is a separate, looser test; the finite difference is one-sided
   and the frontier set is asserted unchanged over the step. The fallback,
   if the fractional-charge SCF proves fragile, is to keep the derivative
   with the structural $Z\times$gap test and make fractional-charge SCF at
   several k-points an explicit error until a milestone with smearing. That
   fallback is raised with the user, not taken silently.
2. **Buffer bands: converge only the needed bands; default of one buffer
   band.** The rule stands, but the draft's evidence for it did not: in
   band-applications 8 bands cost 74 % more than 5 for the same energy, and
   6 bands 17 % more. The draft suggested three buffer bands. The default is
   one, the setting is exposed, and the default is revisited by wall-clock
   measurement on the GPU, recorded in the performance log. The choice of
   one rather than zero or two is mine; the review called "one or two"
   reasonable.
3. **Grid symmetry: an option, not the default.** The condition for diamond
   is $N$ even. The basis offers a grid rule that rounds each $N_i$ up to
   the next FFT-friendly size compatible with a given denominator of the
   fractional translations (2 for diamond). The symmetry tests use it; the
   default rule is unchanged and stays shared with DFTK. The cost of the
   option is the step to the next compatible size, which can be appreciable
   (25 → 30 is 1.7 times the grid points if only the radices 2, 3 and 5 are
   allowed). The name and signature are agreed in the engineering log.
4. **Supercell equivalence: tested**, with explicit FFT grids, the symmetric
   initial density, an assert on the translation invariance of the supercell
   density, and an XC-off variant first. It is the only test that checks the
   k-point weights against something other than DFTK, and it exercises the
   per-atom sum of the nonlocal term and the $\mathbf{G}=0$ bookkeeping at
   a different $\Omega$ and $N_\text{el}$.
5. **Time-reversal reduction: left out of 2b.** It is a pure factor of two
   with no physics attached (see the k-grid section), so it belongs to a
   milestone where cost matters. When it is added, the gap guard and the
   frontier search must run over the representatives with their weights,
   which is the same set of eigenvalues as the unfolded grid.
6. **The grid condition was wrong in the draft.** $4 \mid N$ came from
   reading the fractional translations in cubic coordinates. The draft's
   only negative control, $N = 25$, is odd and fails both rules, so its
   table could not tell them apart. The tests now include $N = 26$.
7. **The projector protocol takes $q^2$**, and the nonlocal term contains no
   square root. `local(q)` keeps its 2a signature; changing it is outside
   this milestone.
8. **The Γ-centred grid is kept**, for the reason given in the k-grid
   section (no density symmetrisation), with its cost now measured. A
   shifted grid with density symmetrisation is a candidate for a later
   milestone and is not designed here.
9. **The gap guard is evaluated at convergence**; the gap over the grid is
   logged in the history at every iteration.
10. **Not adopted or not verified.** The review suggested checking the
    silicon lattice constant of [@yin_cohen1982] against the "overbinds"
    remark; the paper was not consulted, and the remark was removed instead.
    The review did not check the DFTK comparison, the statement that H₂
    needs 80 Ha (that is from the 2a validation document), the 6 s wall
    time, or the $-0.03$ Ha of the gap-guard anecdote, for which it measured
    $-0.063$ Ha at its own setting.
